Composio · App research report

Which of 100 apps are ready to turn into agent tools?

Composio turns apps into tools AI agents can call. Before building a toolkit, you need to know how each app authenticates, whether a developer can sign up alone, what the API looks like, and what blocks shipping. I researched all 100 apps with an agent, checked every answer against the docs, and ranked what is ready to build versus what needs outreach.

01 / Key findings

What stands out across all 100 apps

  1. 01
    Free signup often still blocks shipping to customers

    56 of 100 apps let a developer get credentials for free, but 16 of those still need an app review, marketplace listing, or partner program before you can serve many customers.

  2. 02
    Most apps already ship an official MCP server

    89 of 100 apps publish an official MCP server. 15 of those are not in the Composio catalog yet — ready coverage opportunities.

  3. 03
    Easy wins you can build without a sales call

    66 of 100 apps look ready to integrate today (score 8–10, no partnership gate). 9 of those are still missing from Composio.

  4. 04
    Some apps need outreach no matter how good the API is

    12 of 100 apps require a partnership, sales contact, or partner program before you can build — 5 of those are not in Composio yet. The densest category is Finance and Fintech (4 apps).

  5. 05
    The most common reason an app is hard to integrate

    The most common blocker is getting developer credentials (paid plans, admin approval, or partner signup) (48 of 100 apps, 48%).

  6. 06
    REST and OAuth 2.0 are the default pattern

    91 of 100 apps expose a REST API and 74 support OAuth 2.0 (37 of those still document an extra gate before production). 64 apps offer two or more ways to authenticate.

05 / How I checked accuracy

I labelled 20 apps by hand; automation improved the draft

I hand-checked 20 apps (120 facts) against the real docs. The agent’s first draft scored 52%. After six automated checks it rose to 54%. The final 100% figure includes my corrections and is labelled separately so the automated gain stays honest.

Apps left out of the hand-checked sample

5 apps were kept out of the hand-checked sample (Zoho CRM, Vonage, Squarespace, Paygent Connect, Grain). They are still in the full 100-app dataset; only the accuracy score above was measured on the 20 apps I labelled by hand.

What changed between draft and checked results

  • I corrected FanBasis / Commas domain redirects after confirming the rebrand in public docs.
  • I added six automated checks (schema, live links, quote matching, browser re-read, second-model review, and targeted re-research).
  • I did not retune the first-draft research prompts against the hand-checked answers — verification was added as a separate stage.
  • Overall sample accuracy rose from 52.5% to 54.2% before any human edits to the final dataset.
Every hand-checked answer (120 rows) — draft vs checked vs human label
App Fact My label First draft After checks What happened Which checks
Technical change log (for engineers who want the file-level detail)
  • **Commit `be7d084`**: Added `commas.com` and `commasdocs.com` to `official_domains` for **fanbasis** (app #37, a golden app). During golden labelling it was confirmed that FanBasis, Inc. rebranded to Commas (`fanbasis.com` redirects to `commas.com`, and official API docs moved to `commasdocs.com`). This is an input-data correction, not prompt tuning.
  • **L1 (schema & cross-field rules)** (`agent/loops.py`): Re-validates every claim against Pydantic models and checks 6 cross-field rules (`oauth2_quote`, `access_vs_blocker`, `mcp_yes_has_url`, `gate_official_evidence`, `graphql_quote`, `description_when_docs`). Any L1 failure prevents `supported` status and routes evaluated fields to L6.
  • **L2 (source liveness & official-domain check)** (`agent/loops.py`): Probes evidence URLs (HEAD with streaming GET fallback, disk-cached) and verifies `official_domains` membership for claims tagged with an official tier.
  • **L3 (quote grounding)** (`agent/loops.py`, `agent/evidence.py`): Normalises whitespace/case/smart-quotes/markdown and checks exact substring or `rapidfuzz.partial_ratio >= 90` against cached page text (`httpx.scrape`, `composio_mcp.scrape`, or `exa.snippet`).
  • **L4 (Playwright browser render fallback)** (`agent/tools/browser.py`): Shared headless Chromium renderer triggered only when L3 has empty page text or an ungrounded snippet-only source. On the 100-app run, every evidence URL already had cached page text or snippet text that grounded or resolved without triggering L4 (`claims_checked = 0`).
  • **L5 (independent verifier)** (`agent/verify.py`, `agent/prompts.py`): **Meta Muse Spark** (`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, separate model family from extractor `gpt-6-luna`) judges each non-unknown, non-registry claim strictly against its field definition and the ±1200-char excerpt around its cited quote(s), with no app context beyond the product name.
  • **L6 (targeted re-research)** (`agent/verify.py`, `agent/prompts.py`): For any of the 6 evaluated fields whose pre-L6 status is not `supported` (including `unknown`), runs up to 2 attempts of field-specific Exa queries, single-field re-extraction (`build_field_prompt`), and full L2–L5 re-verification. Candidates are accepted only if grounded by L3/L4 **and** rated `supported` by L5. Contradicted claims whose re-research fails are withdrawn to `unknown`; `main_blocker` runs last using the other verified fields as context.
  • **None to Pass 1 prompts or golden scoring rules.** The verification prompts (`build_verifier_prompt`, `build_field_prompt`) and generic per-field L6 query templates (`L6_QUERIES`) were written from the PRD FR-03/FR-06 field definitions without app-specific hardcoding.
  • **Observed Pass 2 behaviour & honest regression note:**
  • Overall golden accuracy rose from **52.5% (63/120)** in Pass 1 to **54.17% (65/120)** in Pass 2 (**+1.67 pp**).
  • **5 claims fixed** (all via L6 filling pass-1 `unknown` values): HubSpot, Jira, Stripe (`credential_access`: `unknown` → `self_serve_free`), Sherlock (`auth_methods`: `unknown` → `['none']`), Mermaid CLI (`mcp_official`: `unknown` → `no_found`).
  • **3 regressions** (all on `auth_methods`, triggered by L5 marking pass-1 `partially_supported` and L6 replacing the whole multi-value set from a narrower re-research page): DealCloud (`['oauth2', 'api_key', 'bearer_token']` → `['oauth2']`), Snowflake (added `session_other`), PitchBook (`['api_key']` → `['oauth2']`).
  • **6 `abstained_to_wrong` transitions**: L6 filled 6 previously `unknown` claims with grounded values that disagreed with the golden label's classification (Pylon, Mailchimp ×2, Amazon SP-API, Snowflake, Jira).
  • No second Pass 2 iteration was run; Pass 2 is frozen as-is (`data/pass2/`) and reported transparently.

07 / How the agent works

Research first, check second, score without guessing

One model researches each app and must cite a docs quote. A second, independent model helps verify those answers. Readiness scores and the four build groups are calculated in plain code — no model picks the score.

Solid path: research → verify → score → report Dashed panel: six checks on every answer Feedback: weak answers can be researched again

How Composio was used — and where I fell back

Whether each app already has a Composio toolkit comes from the public Composio catalog (1,843 toolkits) — looked up by name, not guessed by a model.

I intended search and page-fetch to run through Composio’s tool layer. The provided consumer key could not authenticate those calls, so I switched the agent to the same search and fetch tools directly, with on-disk caching (1700 research calls, 1922 re-research calls during verification).

Re-run research for one app without cloning anything

Everything a reviewer needs is on this page: findings, evidence, accuracy, and honest misses. If you want to see the agent run live, use the button below. The source repo is optional reading, not required to understand the results.

Live run

Open the GitHub Action, type an app name (for example Linear), and start the workflow. It researches that one app and uploads the result.

Run research on one app
